"Linear Algebra with Applications" is a free and comprehensive textbook that introduces the computational, theoretical, and applied aspects of linear algebra.

The book covers topics such as systems of linear equations, matrices, determinants, vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalization, inner product spaces, orthogonality, and many more. The explanations are accompanied by over 330 worked examples, exercises, and practical applications in geometry, electrical networks, dynamic systems, probability theory, and optimization.

A particularly interesting section discusses how Google's PageRank algorithm uses the dominant eigenvector to rank web pages. The links between websites are represented as a connectivity matrix, and the components of its dominant eigenvector provide an estimate of the relative importance of each page.

This is a very clear example of how an apparently abstract idea from linear algebra can underlie a real-world technology used on a massive scale.

The 2023 edition is available under a Creative Commons license. This is another excellent resource that is worth keeping as a reference.

posts.text:
🔥 NIKE: GET WOKE, GO BROKE?

Nike may be one of the clearest corporate case studies yet.

At its peak in November 2021, Nike traded around $177 per share and was one of the most dominant consumer brands on Earth.

Today, it is trading near $38.

That’s roughly a 78% collapse from the high.

And now Nike has been removed from the S&P 100 after nearly two decades.

But here’s the part that makes this story so interesting:

Nike’s SALES did not immediately collapse.

Revenue actually continued climbing:

2021: $44.5B
2022: $46.7B
2023: $51.2B
2024: $51.4B

So while Nike’s revenue was hitting record highs, investors were already destroying the company’s valuation.

Why?

Beginning years earlier, Nike increasingly transformed itself from a universally recognized sports brand into a company heavily identified with social and political messaging.

The timeline included:

▪️ Colin Kaepernick becoming the centerpiece of a major Nike campaign
▪️ DEI formally becoming a “strategic priority”
▪️ Corporate racial and gender representation targets
▪️ Dylan Mulvaney promoting Nike Women products
▪️ Continued emphasis on transgender and inclusion initiatives
▪️ Controversy surrounding reported Nike support for transgender-athlete research

None of these events alone proves that “wokeness” caused Nike’s collapse.

But that may be the wrong way to look at it.

A brand is an intangible asset.

For decades, Nike’s greatest strength was that almost everyone could wear it.

Republican.
Democrat.
Black.
White.
Male.
Female.
Young.
Old.

The Swoosh didn’t need politics.

It was SPORTS.

Then Nike increasingly inserted itself into some of the most divisive cultural battles in America.

At the exact same time, management was also making enormous strategic mistakes:

▪️ Pulling away from wholesale retailers
▪️ Betting heavily on Direct-to-Consumer
▪️ Losing shelf space
▪️ Falling behind on product innovation
▪️ Allowing Hoka, On and other competitors to explode
▪️ Weakening badly in China

And eventually the financial numbers caught up.

2025 revenue fell roughly 10%.

Nike Digital fell around 20%.

Nike Direct fell around 12% currency-neutral.

By 2026, Nike was attempting a full-scale turnaround.

Perhaps “GET WOKE, GO BROKE” doesn’t mean customers suddenly stop buying your products the morning after a controversial advertisement.

Maybe it happens much more slowly.

A company politicizes its brand.

Part of its audience becomes alienated.

Management becomes increasingly detached from its traditional customer.

Brand loyalty weakens.

Competitors move in.

Strategic mistakes become harder to overcome.

And eventually the numbers follow.

Nike’s revenue peaked YEARS AFTER its stock price did.

That may be the most important clue of all.

The market appears to have begun repricing the value of the Nike brand long before the income statement showed just how serious the deterioration had become.

Now one of the most iconic brands in American history is down roughly 78% from its peak, trading near a 12-year low, and has been kicked out of the S&P 100.

Coincidence?

Bad management?

Cultural alienation?

Or all three feeding into each other?

That’s why I think Nike deserves to be studied as one of the most important “Get Woke, Go Broke” corporate case studies of the last decade.
